“Unless you call Miss Havisham a man. And I doubt even you would go that far.”

“Miss Havisham, uptown?” Joe asked.

“Is there a Miss Havisham downtown?” my sister retorted.

“She wants this boy to go and play at her house. Naturally, he's going. And he'd better play,” she added, shaking her head at me to encourage extreme cheerfulness and high spirits, “or I'll make him.”

I had heard about Miss Havisham uptown—everyone for miles around had heard of her—as an immensely wealthy, grim woman who lived alone in a large, gloomy house barricaded against burglars.

“Well, imagine that!” Joe said in astonishment. “I wonder how she came to know Pip!”

“You fool!” my sister cried. “Who said she knew him?”

“Someone did mention,” Joe politely suggested again, “that she wanted him to come and play.”

“And couldn't she ask Uncle Pumblechook whether he knew a boy who could come and play? Is it just barely possible that Uncle Pumblechook rents property from her and sometimes—we won't say every quarter or half year, since that would ask too much of you—but sometimes goes there to pay his rent? Couldn't she then ask whether he knew a boy to come and play? And couldn't Uncle Pumblechook, who is always thoughtful and considerate towards us—although you may not think so, Joseph,” she said with the deepest reproach, as though Joe were the most unfeeling nephew alive, “mention this boy standing here prancing”—which I solemnly declare I was not—“this boy I've willingly slaved for all my life?”

“Excellent!” Uncle Pumblechook cried. “Well expressed! Exactly to the point! Very good indeed! Now, Joseph, you understand the situation.”

“No, Joseph,” my sister continued reproachfully, while Joe apologetically rubbed the back of his hand repeatedly across his nose. “You don't yet understand it, whatever you may think. You may believe you do, but you do not, Joseph. You don't know that Uncle Pumblechook realizes this visit to Miss Havisham might, for all we know, make the boy's fortune. He has offered to take him into town tonight in his own chaise-cart, put him up for the night, and personally deliver him to Miss Havisham tomorrow morning. And heaven help me!” She tore off her bonnet in sudden despair. “Here I am talking to a pair of idiots, while Uncle Pumblechook waits, the mare catches cold at the door, and the boy stands filthy with soot and dirt from the top of his head to the soles of his feet!”

At Sullivan's Island's latitude, winters are seldom particularly harsh, and in autumn it is very unusual to consider a fire necessary. Yet around the middle of October, 18—, there came an exceptionally chilly day. Shortly before sunset I made my way through the evergreens to my friend's hut. I had not visited him for several weeks, since I then lived in Charleston, nine miles from the island, and transport in both directions was far less convenient than it is now. I knocked on reaching the hut, as usual. When nobody answered, I retrieved the key from its familiar hiding place, unlocked the door, and entered. A splendid fire blazed on the hearth—an unexpected and thoroughly welcome sight. I removed my overcoat, took an armchair beside the crackling logs, and waited patiently for my hosts.

They came home soon after dark and welcomed me most warmly. Jupiter, grinning from ear to ear, hurried about preparing marsh hens for supper. Legrand was in one of his fits of enthusiasm—what else could I call them? He had discovered an unknown bivalve constituting a new genus. More exciting still, with Jupiter's assistance he had hunted down and captured a scarab beetle that he believed entirely new, and he wanted my opinion on it the following morning.

“Why not this evening?” I asked, rubbing my hands over the fire and wishing the whole family of scarab beetles to the devil.

“If only I'd known you were here!” Legrand said. “But it's been so long since I saw you. How could I have predicted that, of all evenings, you'd visit tonight? On my way home I ran into Lieutenant G—— from the fort, and very foolishly lent him the insect. So there's no possibility of your seeing it before morning. Stay the night, and I'll send Jup down to collect it at sunrise. It's the loveliest thing in creation!”

“What is—sunrise?”

“Nonsense, no! The beetle. It's a brilliant gold color, about the size of a large hickory nut, with two jet-black spots near one end of its back and a somewhat longer spot near the other. The antennae are—”

“There isn't any tin in him, Master Will, I keep telling you,” Jupiter interrupted. “He's a gold bug, solid gold, every bit of him, inside and all, except his wings. Never felt a bug half so heavy in my life.”

The two ladies were delighted to see their dear friend again, declared it an age since they had met, and repeatedly asked how she had occupied herself in the meantime. They gave the rest of the family little attention, avoiding Mrs. Bennet whenever possible, speaking only briefly to Elizabeth, and not at all to the others. Soon they were off again, springing from their seats with an energy that startled their brother and hurrying away as if desperate to escape Mrs. Bennet's courtesies.

Every female member of the family found the prospect of the Netherfield ball extremely pleasing. Mrs. Bennet chose to see it as a compliment to her eldest daughter and was especially flattered to receive the invitation from Mr. Bingley himself instead of by formal card. Jane imagined a delightful evening in the company of her two friends, enjoying their brother's attentions. Elizabeth happily anticipated many dances with Mr. Wickham and expected Mr. Darcy's expression and conduct to confirm everything she had heard. Catherine and Lydia's expectations depended less on any particular event or person. Although each, like Elizabeth, planned to dance with Mr. Wickham for half the evening, plenty of other partners would satisfy them too. In any case, a ball was a ball. Even Mary assured the family that she had no reluctance about attending.

“As long as I can keep my mornings to myself, I am content,” she said. “I don't consider it a sacrifice to join in occasional evening engagements. Society makes demands on all of us, and I count myself among those who believe that periods of recreation and amusement are desirable for everyone.”

Elizabeth's spirits were so high that, although she seldom spoke to Mr. Collins unnecessarily, she could not resist asking whether he intended to accept Mr. Bingley's invitation. If he did, would he consider it appropriate to participate in the evening's entertainment? She was rather surprised to find that he had no reservations at all. He was far from fearing any reprimand from either the Archbishop or Lady Catherine de Bourgh if he ventured to dance.

“I certainly do not believe,” he assured her, “that a ball of this sort, hosted by a young man of good character for respectable guests, could have any harmful influence. Indeed, I am so far from objecting to dancing myself that I hope each of my lovely cousins will honor me with a dance during the evening. I therefore take this opportunity to request your hand, Miss Elizabeth, particularly for the first two dances. I trust my cousin Jane will understand the proper reason for this preference and not suppose it indicates any disrespect towards her.”
